questions.title: Heterophyes heterophyes is not cosmopolitan
questions.question: The geographical distribution of the following parasites is cosmopolitan, EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Correct. Heterophyes heterophyes, a small intestinal fluke acquired by eating undercooked brackish-water fish, has a geographically restricted distribution -- the Far East, the Middle East (including Egypt) and parts of the Balkans -- wherever its snail and fish intermediate hosts and local raw-fish-eating habits coincide. This is unlike Ascaris lumbricoides, Hymenolepis nana and Fasciola hepatica, which are found worldwide because their transmission does not depend on a specific brackish-water snail-fish complex. Its restricted distribution is the standard reason it is picked as the exception in a cosmopolitan-distribution list.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fasciola hepatica, transmitted through lymnaeid snails and aquatic vegetation available in many temperate and tropical regions, has a cosmopolitan distribution, not a restricted one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hymenolepis nana, transmitted directly faecal-orally with no obligatory intermediate host, is one of the most widespread cestodes worldwide, so it is cosmopolitan.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ascaris lumbricoides, transmitted by simple faecal-oral ingestion of soil-matured eggs, is among the most cosmopolitan of all human helminths.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Heterophyes heterophyes as geographically restricted rather than cosmopolitan.

questions.title: Hydatid disease is not a common childhood parasite
questions.question: The following parasites affect commonly children, EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Correct. Hydatid disease (Echinococcus granulosus cystic hydatidosis) is acquired by ingesting eggs shed by an infected dog, and because the resulting cyst grows slowly over years before becoming clinically apparent, it is not characteristically a disease of childhood. This is unlike Schistosoma mansoni, Enterobius vermicularis and Hymenolepis nana, which commonly and characteristically affect children through play-related soil/water contact, close-contact autoinfection and poor hand hygiene respectively. The distinction here is epidemiological -- who is typically affected -- not transmission route.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Schistosoma mansoni commonly affects children in endemic areas, who are heavily exposed through swimming and wading in infested fresh water.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Enterobius vermicularis is one of the most common childhood parasitic infections, spread easily among children in close contact (school, household) through autoinfection and airborne/fingernail eggs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hymenolepis nana is the commonest cestode infection of children, favoured by its direct life cycle and poor childhood hand hygiene.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hydatid disease as not characteristically a childhood disease, unlike Schistosoma mansoni, Enterobius vermicularis and Hymenolepis nana.

questions.title: Trichinella spiralis is the viviparous exception
questions.question: The following parasites are oviparous, EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ascaris lumbricoides is oviparous: the adult female lays eggs, which pass out with faeces to mature in soil.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Trichuris trichiura is oviparous, laying barrel-shaped eggs passed in an immature state in faeces.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Enterobius vermicularis is oviparous, laying eggs (deposited on perianal skin rather than in the intestine, but eggs nonetheless).
explanations.D: Correct. Trichinella spiralis is viviparous, not oviparous: the adult female releases live first-stage larvae directly into the host's intestinal mucosa, with no egg stage passed to the outside environment at all. This reproductive difference is why Trichinella diagnosis (muscle biopsy showing encysted larvae, or serology) never looks for an egg, unlike Ascaris, Trichuris or Enterobius. Trichinella shares this viviparous pattern with Dracunculus medinensis and Loa loa, both also tested in this chapter.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Trichinella spiralis as viviparous, unlike the oviparous Ascaris, Trichuris and Enterobius.

questions.title: Oxyuris (Enterobius) is the oviparous exception
questions.question: The following parasites are viviparous, EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Trichinella spiralis is viviparous -- its adult female releases live larvae directly, with no egg stage passed out.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dracunculus medinensis is viviparous -- its gravid female releases live first-stage larvae into water when the skin blister ruptures.
explanations.C: Correct. Oxyuris vermicularis (a synonym for Enterobius vermicularis, the pin-worm) is oviparous, not viviparous: its adult female lays eggs, deposited on perianal skin, that must develop further before becoming infective. This makes it the exception when grouped with Trichinella spiralis, Dracunculus medinensis and Loa loa, all three of which release live larvae directly rather than laying eggs. The oviparous/viviparous split correlates with which stage -- egg or larva -- is the diagnostic finding for each species.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Loa loa is viviparous -- its adult female releases live microfilariae directly into the host's bloodstream.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Oxyuris (Enterobius) vermicularis as oviparous, unlike the viviparous Trichinella, Dracunculus and Loa loa.

questions.title: Guinea worm does not live in the caecum
questions.question: The following helminthes inhabit the caecum, EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pin-worm (Enterobius vermicularis) inhabits the caecum and adjacent large-bowel segments, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Correct. Guinea-worm (Dracunculus medinensis) does not inhabit the caecum, or the intestine at all -- its adult female lives in subcutaneous tissue, most classically of the lower limb. Despite sharing the same 'helminth infecting man' grouping in an exam list with pin-worm and whip-worm, its habitat is entirely extra-intestinal, which is exactly why it is the correct exception here. This is a standard identification trap: not every worm listed alongside intestinal helminths actually lives in the intestine.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Whip-worm (Trichuris trichiura) inhabits the caecum, anchoring by its thin anterior end, so it is not the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Guinea-worm (option B) is the genuine exception, so 'none of the above' is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Identify guinea worm (Dracunculus medinensis) as the exception among caecum-dwelling helminths, since it lives in subcutaneous tissue.

questions.title: Enterobius eggs hatch in the duodenum
questions.question: After ingestion of Enterobius eggs the larvae hatch in the?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gastric acid does not hatch Enterobius eggs; the egg shell is not broken down until the egg reaches the duodenum.
explanations.B: Correct. After a human host swallows an infective Enterobius vermicularis egg, the larva hatches in the duodenum, then migrates onward to mature in the caecum. This duodenal hatching site is a specific, testable fact -- distinct from Ascaris, whose swallowed eggs hatch more generally within the small intestine before the larva begins its hepato-pulmonary migration. Fixing the hatching site to a named segment (duodenum here) is a common exam identification point across this chapter's nematodes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hatching occurs before the larva reaches the jejunum, in the duodenum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hatching occurs well before the ileum, in the duodenum, immediately after the stomach.

questions.subtopic: Life cycle: egg ingestion and hatching
questions.learning_objective: State that ingested Enterobius eggs hatch in the duodenum.

questions.title: Enterobius has no cycle outside the body
questions.question: The worm without cycle outside the body?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ascaris lumbricoides eggs must mature in soil for days to weeks before becoming infective, an obligatory external developmental period.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ancylostoma duodenale eggs hatch in soil and the resulting larvae must moult through several free-living larval stages there before becoming the infective filariform larva, another obligatory external cycle.
explanations.C: Correct. Enterobius vermicularis has an unusually short, direct life cycle: eggs deposited on perianal skin become infective within hours, and can be swallowed again by the same host (retroinfection) or by a close contact almost immediately, with no obligatory period of development in soil. This distinguishes it from Ascaris, Ancylostoma duodenale and Trichuris trichiura, whose eggs must all spend an extended period maturing in the external soil environment before they are infective.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Trichuris trichiura eggs, like Ascaris eggs, require a period of maturation in soil (typically several weeks) before becoming infective, an obligatory external cycle.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Enterobius vermicularis as the nematode without an obligatory external (soil) developmental cycle.

questions.title: Ascaris eggs hatch in the small intestine
questions.question: After ingestion of Ascaris eggs the larvae hatch in the?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gastric acid does not hatch Ascaris eggs; hatching occurs further along the gut, in the small intestine.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The bank's own answer key for this species names the small intestine generally, not the duodenum specifically, distinguishing it from Enterobius's own duodenum-specific hatching fact tested elsewhere in this chapter.
explanations.C: Correct. After a human host swallows an infective Ascaris lumbricoides egg, the larva hatches within the small intestine, from where it penetrates the gut wall to begin its hepato-pulmonary migratory phase before returning to the small intestine as an adult. This small-intestine hatching site is the standard teaching point for Ascaris.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hatching occurs well before the large intestine, within the small intestine, immediately after ingestion and gastric passage.

questions.subtopic: Life cycle: egg ingestion and hatching
questions.learning_objective: State that ingested Ascaris eggs hatch in the small intestine.

questions.title: Trichuris trichiura belongs to Nematoda
questions.question: Trichuris trichiura belongs to?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Trematoda (flukes) are flat, leaf-shaped worms such as Fasciola or Schistosoma; Trichuris is not a fluke.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cestoidea (tapeworms) are flat, segmented, hermaphroditic worms such as Taenia; Trichuris is not a tapeworm.
explanations.C: Correct. Trichuris trichiura is a member of class Nematoda (roundworms) -- an elongated, cylindrical, unsegmented worm with a complete digestive tract and separate sexes. This classification distinguishes it from the flat, segmented Cestoidea (tapeworms) and the flat, leaf-shaped Trematoda (flukes), the other two major helminth classes tested throughout this bank.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nematoda (option C) is the correct class, so 'none of the above' is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Classify Trichuris trichiura as a member of class Nematoda.

questions.title: Dipylidium caninum is not a nematode
questions.question: The following parasites belong to class Nematoda EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Oxyuris (Enterobius) vermicularis is a nematode (roundworm), so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ancylostoma duodenale is a nematode (roundworm), so it is not the exception.
explanations.C: Correct. Dipylidium caninum is a cestode (tapeworm) -- a flat, ribbon-shaped, segmented, hermaphroditic worm -- placing it in class Cestoidea, not Nematoda. This makes it the exception whenever it is listed among genuine roundworms such as Oxyuris vermicularis, Ancylostoma duodenale and Trichostrongylus colubriformis, all of which are true nematodes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Trichostrongylus colubriformis is a nematode (roundworm), so it is not the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Dipylidium caninum as a cestode, not a nematode, unlike Oxyuris, Ancylostoma and Trichostrongylus.

questions.title: Ascaris lumbricoides general biology
questions.question: Ascaris lumbricoides?

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. It is true that Ascaris eggs require a period of soil maturation before becoming infective, but this is only one of three jointly true statements offered, so it is not the single best answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. It is true that Ascaris lumbricoides, at up to 20-35 cm in the female, is the largest (giant) intestinal nematode infecting man, but this is only one of three jointly true statements offered.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. It is true that the Ascaris larva undergoes an obligatory migratory phase (gut wall to liver to lungs to trachea, then swallowed back to the small intestine), but this is only one of three jointly true statements offered.
explanations.D: Correct. Ascaris lumbricoides is correctly described by all three statements together: its egg requires a period of maturation in soil before becoming infective, the adult worm is the largest (giant) intestinal nematode infecting man, and its larva undergoes an obligatory migratory phase before developing into the adult. These are complementary facts about the same species, not competing single-correct options, which is why 'all of the above' is the intended answer.

questions.learning_objective: State that Ascaris lumbricoides requires egg maturation in soil, is the largest intestinal nematode, and has a migratory larval phase.

questions.title: Fertilized Ascaris egg is immature when passed
questions.question: The fertilized egg of Ascaris?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Barrel-shaped describes the Trichuris trichiura egg, not the fertilized Ascaris egg, which is instead rounded/oval.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The fertilized Ascaris egg is brownish (bile-stained), not colourless.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The fertilized Ascaris egg is mamillated -- it has a rough, bile-stained outer coat -- not smooth or without mamillation.
explanations.D: Correct. A fertilized Ascaris lumbricoides egg is unembryonated (immature, a single-cell stage) at the moment it is passed in the host's faeces. Further embryonation to the infective larvated stage happens afterward in soil, not before or at the time of passage, which is why freshly stool-passed Ascaris eggs are not yet infective to a new host. This immaturity at passage is a standard descriptive point distinguishing when an egg becomes infective from when it is shed.

questions.learning_objective: State that the fertilized Ascaris lumbricoides egg is immature (unembryonated) when passed in faeces.

questions.title: Enterobius vermicularis is called the pin worm
questions.question: Enterobius vermicularis?

explanations.A: Correct. Enterobius vermicularis is called the pin-worm, its slender, pin-like tapering tail giving the common name. It has no larval migratory phase through the lungs, unlike Ascaris, hookworm and Strongyloides, and its eggs are already laid embryonated (mature, near-infective) on perianal skin by the gravid female, not laid immature -- making the other three options each false for this species. The pin-worm/whip-worm naming distinction is the most frequently tested identification point for this species.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Whip-worm is the common name for Trichuris trichiura, whose thin, whip-like anterior end gives that name, not Enterobius vermicularis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Enterobius vermicularis has no larval migratory phase through the lungs, unlike Ascaris, hookworm and Strongyloides.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Enterobius eggs are laid already embryonated (near-mature, close to infective) on perianal skin, becoming infective within hours -- not laid immature the way Ascaris or Trichuris eggs are.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Enterobius vermicularis as the pin-worm, with no larval migratory phase.

questions.title: Trichuris trichiura egg is barrel-shaped, brownish and immature
questions.question: Egg of Trichuris trichiura?

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. It is true that the Trichuris egg is barrel- (lemon-) shaped with bipolar mucoid plugs, but this is only one of three jointly true descriptors offered.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. It is true that the Trichuris egg is brownish (bile-stained), but this is only one of three jointly true descriptors offered.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. It is true that the Trichuris egg is an immature (unembryonated) ovum when passed, but this is only one of three jointly true descriptors offered.
explanations.D: Correct. The egg of Trichuris trichiura is barrel- (lemon-) shaped with bipolar mucoid plugs at each end, brownish in colour (bile-stained), and immature (a single-cell, unembryonated ovum) at the time it is passed in the host's faeces. These three descriptive facts are jointly true and are combined here into one 'all of the above' item testing complete egg recognition, distinguishing it from the differently shaped Ascaris and Enterobius eggs.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Trichuris trichiura egg is barrel-shaped, brownish, and immature when passed.

questions.title: Enterobius does not lay eggs in the intestine
questions.question: The following parasites lay eggs in the intestine EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ascaris lumbricoides lays its eggs directly into the intestinal lumen, from where they pass out with faeces, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Correct. Enterobius vermicularis is the exception: the gravid female migrates out through the anus at night and deposits her eggs on the perianal skin, not into the intestinal lumen. This is why routine stool examination is an unreliable diagnostic method for Enterobius, and a perianal (cellophane tape) swab is used instead -- unlike Ascaris, Trichuris and Ancylostoma duodenale, all of which lay their eggs directly in the gut lumen and are readily diagnosed by ordinary stool examination.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Trichuris trichiura lays its eggs directly into the intestinal lumen (caecum and adjacent bowel), so it is not the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ancylostoma duodenale lays its eggs directly into the small-intestinal lumen, so it is not the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Enterobius vermicularis as the exception that does not lay its eggs in the intestinal lumen.

questions.title: Necator americanus belongs to Nematoda
questions.question: Necator americanus belong to?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Trematoda (flukes) are flat, leaf-shaped worms; Necator americanus is not a fluke.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cestoidea (tapeworms) are flat, segmented, hermaphroditic worms; Necator americanus is not a tapeworm.
explanations.C: Correct. Necator americanus, the 'New World' hookworm, is a member of class Nematoda (roundworms) -- an elongated, cylindrical, unsegmented worm with a complete digestive tract and separate sexes. This is the same class as Trichuris trichiura, tested elsewhere in this chapter, and distinct from the flat, segmented Cestoidea (tapeworms) that a species such as Dipylidium caninum belongs to instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 'Tape worms' names Cestoidea, not the class Necator americanus belongs to; a hookworm is not a tapeworm.

questions.learning_objective: Classify Necator americanus as a member of class Nematoda.
